# The position--label fibre is generated by adjacent four-cycles and tight six-cycles

Date: 2026-07-27

This note separates three questions which were being conflated:

1. linear conservation of rooted position--label histograms;
2. saturation of the corresponding integral lattice; and
3. chronological reachability by literal collar packets with coefficient-one
   middle ownership.

The second question has a positive answer **for every admitted pair of
position colours**, and hence for the full fibre if the admitted
colour-pair graph is connected.  The presently certified literal
packets do not yet give that connectedness: boundary rectangles act on
their two boundary positions, while the three-top packet acts on
position three and a remote position.  The third question does not
follow from the lattice statement.
There is also a useful correction: the universal four-top left-rotation
recharge does **not** preserve the position--label histogram, so that
histogram is an invariant of the two-column three-top and two-top packets,
not of every recharge primitive presently in the files.

## 1. The membership-edge-colouring model

Put \(X=[2m]\), \(M=m+H\), and let \(G=G_{2m,M}\) be the bipartite
membership graph with parts

\[
 {\cal U}=\binom X M,\qquad X,
\]

and edge set

\[
 E(G)=\{(U,v):U\in{\cal U},\ v\in U\}.
\]

A rooted word on every top is the same thing as a colouring

\[
                         c:E(G)\longrightarrow [M]
\tag{1.1}
\]

such that the \(M\) edges incident with each \(U\in{\cal U}\) receive
all \(M\) colours once.  The colour of \((U,v)\) is the rooted position
occupied by \(v\) in the word on \(U\).

For a colour (j) and label (v), put

\[
 h_{j,v}(c)=\#\{U\ni v:c(U,v)=j\}.
\tag{1.2}
\]

These are the global rooted position--label histograms.

### Lemma 1.1 (the packets are Kempe cycles)

Fix two rooted positions (p,q).

1. A two-top boundary rectangle on adjacent tops (U,U'), swapping
   common labels (a,b) in opposite directions, is the alternating
   four-cycle

   \[
        U-a-U'-b-U
   \tag{1.3}
   \]

   in (G).
2. A three-top re-root packet on

   \[
    C+\{x,y\},\quad C+\{x,a\},\quad C+\{a,y\}
   \]

   is the alternating tight six-cycle

   \[
   C+xy-x-C+xa-a-C+ay-y-C+xy .
   \tag{1.4}
   \]

Both switches preserve every (h_{j,v}).

#### Proof

For (1.3), the old (p,q) entries are (a,b) on the first row and
(b,a) on the second; the new shore interchanges the two colours along
the displayed four-cycle.

For (1.4), after aligning the retained roots as in the three-top
theorem, the two relevant columns are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc|cc}
 &\multicolumn{2}{c|}{\rm old}&\multicolumn{2}{c}{\rm new}\\
 &p&q&p&q\\ \hline
 C+xy&x&y&y&x\\
 C+xa&a&x&x&a\\
 C+ay&y&a&a&y.
\end{array}
\tag{1.5}
\]

This is precisely the two-colour switch on (1.4).  At each right
vertex (x,a,y), one (p)-edge and one (q)-edge are merely
interchanged, proving (1.2) is fixed. \(
\square\)

The physical hypotheses in the existing rectangle and three-top
theorems ensure that every structural cycle in (1.3)--(1.4) can be
equipped with the required arms and fillers when their stated bounds
on (m,H) hold.  The assertion here is only about the incidence
projection, not simultaneous installation of all those equipments.

## 2. The cycle lattice of the membership graph

Orient every edge of (G) from ({\cal U}) to (X), and write
(Z_1(G;\mathbb Z)) for its integral cycle lattice.

### Theorem 2.1 (small-cycle generation)

Assume (H\ge3).  The integral cycle lattice (Z_1(G;\mathbb Z)) is
generated by

* the adjacent-top four-cycles (1.3); and
* the common-core tight six-cycles (1.4).

In particular this generating sublattice is saturated.

#### Proof

We use three reductions.

**Arbitrary four-cycles.**  Let (U-a-V-b-U) be any four-cycle, so
(a,b\in U\cap V).  The Johnson graph on the (M)-sets containing
(a,b) is connected.  Choose a path

\[
                         U=U_0,U_1,\ldots,U_t=V
\]

inside it.  Consecutive tops are adjacent and still contain (a,b).
The arbitrary four-cycle is the telescoping signed sum of

\[
                         U_i-a-U_{i+1}-b-U_i,
\]

so it is generated by (1.3).

**Arbitrary six-cycles.**  Write one as

\[
 U_0-x-U_1-a-U_2-y-U_0.
\tag{2.1}
\]

Choose an ((M-2))-set (C) disjoint from (x,a,y); this is possible
because (2m-3\ge M-2).  Use the preceding four-cycle reduction to
replace, in the cycle lattice, (U_0,U_1,U_2) respectively by

\[
 C+xy,\qquad C+xa,\qquad C+ay,
\]

while retaining the relevant pair of incident right vertices.  What
remains is exactly the tight six-cycle (1.4).

**Long cycles.**  Consider a simple cycle with at least four left
vertices and three consecutive left vertices (U_0,U_1,U_2).  Since

\[
                 |U_0\cap U_2|\ge 2M-2m=2H\ge6,
\]

we may choose (w\in U_0\cap U_2) distinct from the four right
vertices incident with (U_0) and (U_2) on the original cycle.
The two-edge path (U_0-w-U_2) cuts off a six-cycle.  The complementary
closed walk has fewer edges; if (w) was already a remote right vertex
of the original cycle, split that closed walk at its repeated (w).
Induction on edge count reduces the original cycle to four- and
six-cycles.  The first two reductions finish the proof.

Every integral circulation of a graph is an integral sum of oriented
simple cycles.  Hence the displayed generators give all of
\(Z_1(G;\mathbb Z)\), proving saturation. \(\square\)

## 3. Saturation of the full histogram fibre

Let (z_{e,j}\in\mathbb Z) be a signed change of the colour table.
The linearized fixed-fibre conditions are

\[
 \sum_jz_{e,j}=0\quad(e\in E(G)),
 \qquad
 \sum_{e\ni w}z_{e,j}=0
       \quad(w\in {\cal U}\sqcup X,\ j\in[M]).
\tag{3.1}
\]

The left-vertex equations fix one occurrence of every position on every
top, the right-vertex equations fix (1.2), and the edge equations keep
each label in its original top.

### Corollary 3.1 (integral fibre theorem, conditional on the colour graph)

Let \(\Gamma\) be the graph on rooted positions in which \(p q\) is an
edge when both the adjacent four-cycle and tight six-cycle switches are
available for the colour pair \(p,q\).  On each connected component of
\(\Gamma\), after also fixing for every membership edge \(e\) the
quantity
\(\sum_{j\ {\rm in\ that\ component}}x_{e,j}\), the resulting fibre
lattice is generated by the corresponding four- and six-cycles.  In
particular, if \(\Gamma\) is connected, the whole lattice (3.1) is
generated and there is no further **linear** capacity cut in the rooted
position--label margins.

#### Proof

For a fixed colour \(j\), \(z^{(j)}=(z_{e,j})_e\) is an integral
circulation of \(G\).  In one component of \(\Gamma\), choose a spanning
tree and a reference colour \(j_0\).  By Theorem 2.1, express every
\(z^{(j)}\), \(j\ne j_0\), as an integral sum of the small graph cycles
and transfer those cycles along the unique colour-tree path from
\(j_0\) to \(j\).  The edge equations in (3.1) give

\[
                      z^{(j_0)}=-\sum_{j\ne j_0}z^{(j)},
\]

so these transfers produce all of \(z\). \(\square\)

This is an integral-lattice statement.  It does **not** assert that a
decomposition can be ordered so that every intermediate colour table
is (0)-(1), nor that the long collar contexts required by the
physical packets are present when needed.  In algebraic-statistics
language, saturation of the move lattice has been proved; the stronger
Markov-basis/chronological-connectivity statement remains open.

### Certified-palette update

In the literal theorems currently on file, a boundary rectangle swaps
its two exposed boundary positions, while the matched-cut three-top
packet swaps position three with one remote position.  The separate
twelve-top bidirectional theorem constructs a histogram-neutral paired
left/right recharge which moves labels across every adjacent pair of
rooted positions.  It therefore connects these components in
\(\Gamma\).

Accordingly the admitted-position graph obstruction is now closed at
the bounded-packet level.  Theorem 2.1 still does not by itself prove
the literal all-position Markov-basis statement: the universal
four-top left rotation alone leaves the histogram fibre (Proposition
6.1 below), while the twelve-top replacement needs its complete
coefficient-one source shore to be currently present.

## 4. Three-top moves alone are not saturated on the stated fibre

There is a stronger invariant when four-cycle rectangles are omitted.
For (A\in\binom X{M-1}), define the position--deletion histogram

\[
 d_{j,A}(c)=\#\{v\notin A:c(A+v,v)=j\}.
\tag{4.1}
\]

### Proposition 4.1 (deletion-histogram obstruction)

Every tight three-top six-cycle preserves all (d_{j,A}).  There are
two word tables with identical position--label histograms which differ
in (\Theta(N)) deletion-histogram coordinates, where
(N=\binom{2m}{M}).  Consequently deleting (o(N)) exceptional tops
does not make the three-top lattice saturated on a position--label
fibre.

#### Proof

At column (p), the old deletion remainders in (1.5) are

\[
                         C+y,\quad C+x,\quad C+a,
\]

and the new remainders are the same three sets in cyclic order.  The
same holds at (q), proving invariance.

For the quantitative counterexample, fix four labels (a,b,x,y).
Pair every top of the form

\[
 S+x\quad\hbox{with}\quad S+y,
 \qquad a,b\in S,\quad x,y\notin S,
\]

where (|S|=M-1).  This gives

\[
                         \binom{2m-4}{M-3}=\Theta(N)
\]

disjoint adjacent-top pairs.  Put (a,b) in positions (p,q) in one
order on the first top and the opposite order on the second, then apply
the four-cycle switch to every pair.  The global position--label
histograms are unchanged.  At position (p), however, each pair
changes the four distinct coordinates

\[
 (S+x)-a,\quad(S+x)-b,\quad(S+y)-a,\quad(S+y)-b.
\]

Positive and negative coordinates from different pairs cannot cancel:
sets obtained by deleting (a) contain (b) but not (a), while sets
obtained by deleting (b) contain (a) but not (b), and within each
class the parent top is recovered uniquely.  The resulting
(\ell_1)-difference is (\Theta(N)).  Removing one top deletes only
O(1) of these charges, so an (o(N)) exceptional set cannot erase the
obstruction. \(
\square\)

Thus the adjacent two-top rectangle is not merely convenient: it kills
a genuine extensive invariant of the three-top system.

## 5. A canonical fibre and its exact missing-colour tax

The stronger invariant (4.1) is not itself a capacity obstruction.  It
has a canonical near-flat initialization.

Let \(G^\downarrow\) be the bipartite graph between \(M\)-sets \(U\)
and \((M-1)\)-sets \(A\), with edge \(U A\) when \(A\subset U\).
Its two degrees are

\[
                 \deg(U)=M,\qquad
                 \deg(A)=q:=2m-M+1=m-H+1<M.
\tag{5.1}
\]

### Lemma 5.1 (proper deletion-colour initialization)

There is a word table for which

\[
                         d_{j,A}\in\{0,1\}
\tag{5.2}
\]

for every position \(j\) and every \((M-1)\)-set \(A\).

#### Proof

By König's line-colouring theorem, \(G^\downarrow\) has a proper
edge-colouring with its maximum degree \(M\).  At an \(M\)-set \(U\),
the \(M\) incident edges receive all \(M\) colours, so colour \(j\)
specifies the unique deleted label \(v=U\setminus A\) occupying
position \(j\).  Properness at \(A\) is exactly (5.2). \(\square\)

In this normal form, a tight three-top packet is an alternating
six-cycle in \(G^\downarrow\) as well as in the top--label graph.  For
two colours \(p,t\), the \(p,t\)-subgraph of \(G^\downarrow\) is a
disjoint union of paths and even cycles.  A literal tight packet is a
component of length six.

There is an exact unavoidable endpoint tax.  Put
\(\kappa=M-q=2H-1\).  For a colour \(p\), let \(I_p\) be the set of
right vertices \(A\) incident with a \(p\)-edge.  Since every \(A\)
sees exactly \(q\) distinct colours,

\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \sum_{t\ne p}|I_p\setminus I_t|
 =\sum_{A\in I_p}(M-q)
 =\kappa N .
 \quad}
\tag{5.3}
\]

Thus, summed over the \(M-1\) possible partners \(t\), at least
\(\kappa N\) base-colour incidences are forced to be path endpoints
rather than members of alternating cycles.  This is only an
\(O(H/m)\) fraction: the capacity scale left by (5.3) is
\(M-O(H)=m-O(H)\) cyclic partner directions per typical top, exactly
the scale of the local re-root theorem.

Hence the deletion invariant explains the forced \(O(H)\) loss but
does not rule out factor-\(m\) global recycling.  What remains is to
force most surviving two-colour cycles to have length six (and then to
install their collar contexts), rather than generic long length.  This
is a simultaneous short-cycle factorization problem for the \(M\)
König matchings of \(G^\downarrow\).

## 6. Correction concerning the four-top recharge

The arbitrary-word four-top theorem performs left rotation on four
words (p_i).  In its notation, the old position-one multiset is

\[
                         \{v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3\},
\]

whereas after rotation the new position-one multiset is the multiset of
the first letters of (F_0,F_1,F_2,F_3), namely

\[
                         \{A_1,B_1,A_1,B_1\}.
\]

The data may be chosen so these multisets differ.  Hence:

### Proposition 6.1

The global position--label histogram is **not** invariant under the
universal four-top left-rotation recharge currently proved in
`MATH_THEOREM_L_COLLAR_NEUTRAL_REROOTING_AND_LINEAR_LOCAL_REUSE_20260727.md`.

Any claim of a common histogram invariant must therefore either omit
that primitive or redefine "rooted position" using an absolute phase
which co-rotates with the word.  The latter convention is not the
relative rooted-position convention used to obtain the local directions
(T^kp) in that theorem.

## 7. Capacity and the remaining chronology gate

The lattice theorem rules out a linear histogram obstruction, but it
does not install helpers.  A useful calibration is available before
collars are imposed.  Give every top an independent uniform word.  Fix
a focal top (U), positions (p,q), and the focal labels
(x=c(U,p),y=c(U,q)).  Adjacent tops which still contain (x,y) number

\[
                         (M-2)(2m-M).
\]

For each such top (V),

\[
 \Pr[c(V,p)=y,\ c(V,q)=x]=\frac1{M(M-1)}.
\tag{6.1}
\]

Thus the expected number of raw opposite-orientation rectangle
companions for one prescribed focal transposition is

\[
 \frac{(M-2)(2m-M)}{M(M-1)}=1+o(1).
\tag{6.2}
\]

For each prescribed \(q\), independence of the candidate helper words
gives

\[
 \Pr[\hbox{at least one companion}]
 =1-\left(1-\frac1{M(M-1)}\right)^{(M-2)(2m-M)}
 =1-e^{-1}+o(1).
\]

Consequently the expected number of distinct successful choices among
the \(M-1\) values of \(q\) is
\((1-e^{-1}+o(1))M\).  (For fixed \(p\), one helper top can be opposite
for at most one focal \(q\).)  Thus the raw incidence model has order
\(M\) available directions per focal top; there is no evident counting
deficit at the histogram level.

What (6.2) omits is precisely the remaining hard gate.  A physical
rectangle or re-root packet prescribes radius-(2H) arms, phase cuts,
and a squarefree coefficient-one middle-owner shore.  Those data are
not recorded by (1.1).  Each proved packet preserves coefficient one
when its complete source shore is present, so coefficient-one ownership
adds no new linear equation to (3.1); it adds (0)-(1) availability
and disjointness constraints.  A signed lattice decomposition can use
the same top with incompatible words and hence need not admit a legal
ordering.

The exact remaining statement is therefore a **positive chronological
lifting theorem**:

> realize a required (\Theta(W))-term small-cycle decomposition by a
> sequence of currently present collar-equipped source cycles, while
> keeping one word per top and coefficient-one middle ownership, after
> discarding only (o(N)) tops.

This note proves that such a theorem cannot fail for an additional
linear position--label invariant.  It does not prove the theorem.
